Where is Manchester, and how big is it?

Manchester is the largest city in New Hampshire, on the Merrimack River in the south-central part of the state. It is one of two county seats of Hillsborough County, along with Nashua.

The city covers 34.93 square miles, 33.07 of them land. It lies 18 miles south of Concord, 18 miles north of Nashua and 51 miles north-northwest of Boston. The Merrimack and Piscataquog rivers and Cohas Brook drain it, and Massabesic Lake forms the eastern border. Wellington Hill, at 570 feet, is the high point.

The 2020 census counted 115,644 residents, and the Census Bureau estimates 116,818 for July 1, 2025. Hillsborough County as a whole had 422,937 people in 2020.

What are Manchester's neighborhoods?

Manchester's 2010 Master Plan defines 25 neighborhoods, though none has legal or political authority and only some have associations. Buyers and agents still use the names, so they show up in how a house is described.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame and McGregorville, and Piscataquog (Granite Square)
  • East Side: North End, Janeville and Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Periphery: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

Because the city is one school district and one tax jurisdiction, the neighborhood does not change your tax rate. It changes who is likely to buy, what the lot looks like and how close you are to the mills, downtown or the highway.

What shaped Manchester's housing stock?

Textile mills built much of Manchester. John Goffe III settled beside Cohas Brook in 1722, the area was chartered as Derryfield in 1751, and it was renamed Manchester in 1810. The Amoskeag Manufacturing Company's company town was founded on the eastern bank in 1838, and Manchester became a city in 1846.

Mill No. 11 was 900 feet long and held 4,000 looms, once the largest cotton mill in the world. About 17,000 workers struck for nine months in 1922, and Amoskeag filed for bankruptcy in 1935. The 1936 flood destroyed the McGregor Bridge and caused $2.5 million in damage.

Many of the houses near the old mills date from this boom, including multi-family buildings. An older multi-family building can bring deferred repairs and tenant questions into the same sale.

Who are the largest employers in Manchester?

Healthcare, education, finance and technology now anchor Manchester's economy, and the mill complexes host offices instead of looms. The employer figures below are from a 2017 count for the Manchester area, so treat them as a snapshot.

Employer (2017)Employees
Elliot Hospital3,682
Catholic Medical Center2,600
Southern New Hampshire University2,093
Eversource Energy1,400
Saint Anselm College689

Retail centers on downtown, South Willow Street (NH Route 28) and Second Street (NH Route 3A), and the Mall of New Hampshire opened in 1977 with more than 125 stores.

What weather should a Manchester seller plan for?

Manchester has cold, snowy winters and hot, humid summers. The mean daily temperature is 25.6 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 73.8 in July, with 26 to 30 days a year at or above 90 and about three days at or below zero.

Annual precipitation averages 40.39 inches. The record high is 103 degrees, set July 22, 2011, and the record low is minus 29 in February 1943. The 1936 flood shows the rivers can rise, and New Hampshire's seller disclosure form asks about flood hazard zones. If your house is near the river, Piscataquog or Cohas Brook, check the flood zone status before you answer that question.

How do roads, flights and buses serve Manchester?

Interstates 93 and 293 meet near the Mall of New Hampshire, and I-93 is being widened to eight lanes from Salem to Manchester. The city has two interstates, one U.S. route and six state routes.

Manchester-Boston Regional Airport is the fourth-largest passenger airport and third-largest cargo airport in New England. The Manchester Transit Authority runs local bus routes plus three regional Zip Line express routes to Concord, Nashua and Salem, and Greyhound provides intercity service. Passenger trains ended in 1967, and an Amtrak Boston to Concord service with a Manchester stop has been proposed for 2035.

Airport and highway access is a selling point for a house, while the rail proposal is only a plan.

How are Manchester property taxes calculated?

Manchester's 2025 tax rate is $20.24 per $1,000, and the city lists a 2025 assessment ratio of 64.8%. The rate has four parts.

Component (2025)Rate per $1,000
Municipal10.04
County1.36
Local education7.33
State education1.51
Total20.24

The tax year runs April 1 to March 31, and bills go out twice. The first is mailed late May or early June and the second in mid to late November, each due 30 days after mailing. The first bill uses half of the prior year's rate, and the state sets the new rate in October or November before the second bill.

What happens if Manchester taxes are not paid?

Manchester charges 8% a year on delinquent taxes under RSA 76:13, and unpaid balances can move to a lien. A notice of impending lien goes out by certified mail at least 30 days before the lien is executed, and interest then runs at 14% a year.

If taxes stay unpaid two years after the lien, the tax collector can execute a tax deed to the city under RSA 80:76. A former owner who wants to buy the property back after the deed must pay back taxes, interest, costs and a penalty of 10% of the equalized assessed value. The city also charges $10 per property for lien-release research and $2 per receipt. Selling before a lien is executed is a way to avoid the 14% rate and the deed risk.

Does Manchester require a certificate for rental houses?

Yes. The city requires every residential rental property to have a Certificate of Compliance under Chapter 150, the Housing Code, of its Code of Ordinances. An application is required for any new, vacant or previously owner-occupied residential rental that is to be rented or offered for rent.

If you own a rental with a valid certificate and sell it, a Transfer of Ownership form assigns the certificate to the new owner. The Building Department asks for the form with a $50 check payable to the City of Manchester, and it is not accepting these applications electronically. Housing inspections are by appointment only, at 603-624-6450.

That rule affects how a landlord sells. A buyer who wants to rent the house has to deal with the certificate, so confirm yours is current before you list it.

What does a Manchester seller pay at closing, and what must be disclosed?

New Hampshire's real estate transfer tax is $.75 per $100 on both buyer and seller under RSA 78-B, filed through Granite Tax Connect. On a $450,000 sale, each side's share is $3,375.

The seller of a one to four family home must disclose, in writing, the private water and sewage systems, insulation, any federally designated flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank, under RSA 477:4-d. For an assessment you believe is too high, the abatement application is due to the city by March 1 after the final bill, and an appeal must be filed by September 1.

How does a cash sale work in Manchester?

A cash sale lets a Manchester owner sell the house as-is, skipping repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal. You share details, receive an offer and decide whether to accept.

More questions about Manchester, NH

What is Manchester's 2025 property tax rate?

It is $20.24 per $1,000 of assessed value, made up of $10.04 municipal, $1.36 county, $7.33 local education and $1.51 state education. The 2025 assessment ratio is 64.8%.

When are Manchester tax bills due?

Bills are mailed twice a year, around late May or early June and again in mid to late November. Each is due 30 days after mailing.

Do I need a Certificate of Compliance to sell a rental in Manchester?

If the property is a rental with a valid certificate, the new owner needs a Transfer of Ownership form and a $50 fee to take it over. A new owner who rents a previously owner-occupied house needs a new application.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax?

The statute taxes both buyer and seller at $.75 per $100 of the price. Your contract and closing agent set out who pays which share.

How long can Manchester wait before taking a house for unpaid taxes?

The tax collector can execute a tax deed to the city two years after a lien, if taxes remain unpaid, after notice to owners and mortgagees.

Where is Nashua, and what does the city cover?

Nashua is in southern New Hampshire, in southeastern Hillsborough County, and borders Middlesex County, Massachusetts, to the south. It is one of Hillsborough County's two county seats, with Manchester, and the second-largest city in northern New England.

The city covers 31.73 square miles, of which 30.83 are land. The Merrimack River forms the eastern boundary, the Nashua River roughly bisects the city and Pennichuck Brook forms the northern boundary. Gilboa Hill, at 426 feet, is the highest point. The 2020 census counted 91,322 residents, and the Census Bureau estimates 92,435 for July 1, 2025.

The Massachusetts line is close, which shapes who shops and who buys here. South Nashua's commercial district, anchored by Pheasant Lane Mall, draws Massachusetts shoppers because New Hampshire has no sales tax.

What are the main areas of Nashua?

Nashua is usually described by district, and each has a different housing feel. The areas below are the ones that come up most when owners describe where a house sits.

  • Downtown, centered on Main Street, the oldest commercial district
  • The Tree Streets, a neighborhood near downtown reached by the Broad Street Parkway
  • The Millyard, the former mill district and the Nashua Manufacturing Company Historic District
  • French Hill, the northern area once called Nashville
  • The Amherst Street corridor (NH 101A) in the northwest
  • South Nashua, near the Massachusetts line

If your house is in or beside a historic district, ask the city what review applies before you plan exterior work as a pre-sale fix.

How did Nashua become Nashua?

The area was settled around 1654 to 1655 as a fur-trading town within the Massachusetts tract called Dunstable. The New Hampshire part was incorporated as Dunstable in 1746 and renamed Nashua in 1836, after the river. The city was incorporated in 1853.

The Nashua Manufacturing Company and the Jackson Manufacturing Company were incorporated in 1823 and 1824, and mills drove the city until the last nearby mill closed in 1949. Sanders Associates, now part of BAE Systems, moved into a closed mill. An employee there, Ralph Baer, developed the Magnavox Odyssey, the first commercial home video game system. Digital Equipment Corporation arrived in the 1970s and tied Nashua to the Boston-area technology corridor.

What does the Nashua economy rest on?

Nashua has moved from textiles to financial and professional services, high technology and defense. Employers and sites named for the city include BAE Systems, Dell and Oracle, plus the Boston Air Route Traffic Control Center.

Nashua Technology Park occupies a former Digital Equipment campus. Two major medical centers, Southern New Hampshire Medical Center and St. Joseph Hospital, are in the city.

How do cold winters and wet springs affect a Nashua house?

Nashua has a humid continental climate, with a January mean of 24.1 degrees Fahrenheit and a July mean of 72.7. It averages about 48.2 inches of precipitation and about 52.9 inches of snow a year.

Between 26 and 30 days a year reach 90 degrees or higher, and about 8.7 days fall below zero. A buyer's inspector will usually look at:

  • Roof condition after snow and ice
  • Basement moisture and lot drainage
  • Heating equipment and fuel storage
  • Insulation, which the state disclosure form asks about

How do you get around Nashua?

The Everett Turnpike is the main highway, and U.S. 3 follows it from the Massachusetts border to Exit 7E. NH 101A (Amherst Street), NH 111 (Hollis Street), NH 111A and NH 130 (Broad Street) also serve the city. The Broad Street Parkway, completed in 2015, connects Exit 6 to downtown and gives Nashua a third crossing of the Nashua River.

The Nashua Transit System operates nine bus routes. Boston Express runs from the Nashua Transit Center, near Exit 8, to South Station and Logan Airport. Nashua Airport (Boire Field) handles general aviation only, so air travelers use Manchester-Boston Regional or Logan. The state has studied extending the MBTA Lowell Line to Manchester, with proposed Nashua stops, but the project awaits federal funding.

What is Nashua's property tax rate?

Nashua's 2025 tax rate is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up from $15.90 in 2024. That is an increase of 93 cents, or 5.83 percent, according to the Nashua Telegraph's report on the state-certified rate.

ItemNashua fact
2025 rate$16.83 per $1,000
2024 rate$15.90 per $1,000
Tax yearApril 1 to March 31
First billDue July 1, estimated at 50% of prior year's rate
Second billMailed November 14, 2025, due December 15, 2025
Abatement deadlineMarch 1

The paper reported that total property values rose by about $100 million, less than one percent, so the higher rate did not come from a big valuation jump. It did not break the rate into city, school and county shares.

How are Nashua taxes handled when a house is sold?

Nashua says property taxes are prorated by day from April 1 when a home is bought or sold. The first installment is due July 1 and the second is due when the state sets the rate, generally no later than December 20.

If you sold the property but still receive a bill, the Tax Collector asks you to forward it to the current owner, or to return it in the envelope with a note on the sale date and the buyer. A new owner may see the old name for a while, since the Registry of Deeds has to send the transfer to the Assessor's Office. Taxes can be looked up online through the city's property tax self-service portal.

How do you challenge a Nashua assessment?

Ask the Assessor's Office, at 603-589-3040, to review the data and then file a written abatement application by March 1. If you miss March 1, no action can be taken for the current tax year.

You may still ask for a spring review, in which the Assessing Department may review your value for the following tax year. State rules then set the path: the city has until July 1 to respond, and an appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, not both, is due by September 1. The abatement does not stop collection, so pay the bill. A homeowner planning to sell should decide early whether the effort is worth it, since a buyer will care more about future bills than a past refund.

What costs and disclosures apply when selling in Nashua?

The New Hampshire transfer tax is $.75 per $100 on each of the buyer and the seller, under RSA 78-B. On a $500,000 sale that is $3,750 each. The tax is filed through Granite Tax Connect.

For a one to four family home, the seller must disclose in writing the private water and sewage systems, insulation, any federally designated flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank, under RSA 477:4-d.

How does a cash sale work in Nashua?

A cash sale in Nashua means you describe the house, receive an offer and choose whether to accept, without repairs or a lender appraisal. The steps that remain are the title search, tax proration and the state transfer tax.

More questions about Nashua, NH

What is the Nashua tax rate for 2025?

It is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up from $15.90 in 2024, according to the Nashua Telegraph's report on the state-set rate.

When are Nashua property tax bills due?

The first bill is due July 1 and is based on half of the prior year's rate. The second bill for 2025 was mailed November 14 and due December 15, 2025.

Are Nashua property taxes prorated when I sell?

Yes. The city says taxes are prorated by day from April 1 for a home that is bought or sold. Your closing agent will show the figure.

What if I missed the March 1 abatement deadline in Nashua?

No action can be taken for that tax year. You may request a spring review, which may lead to a review of your value for the following year.

Is there a sales tax or transfer tax on a Nashua house sale?

New Hampshire has a real estate transfer tax of $.75 per $100 on each of the buyer and the seller. The state has no general sales tax, according to the encyclopedia entry on the city's shopping district.

Selling in Concord?

Where is Concord, and how is the city laid out?

Concord is the capital of New Hampshire and the county seat of Merrimack County, in the south-central part of the state. It covers 67.19 square miles, about 16 miles north of Manchester and 66 miles north of Boston.

The city is bigger on the map than its population suggests, so a Concord address can mean very different things. Downtown includes the North End and South End neighborhoods, and four villages sit around it:

  • Penacook
  • Concord Heights
  • East Concord
  • West Concord

Most homes are in the Concord School District, but the Penacook area is served by the Merrimack Valley School District. That split matters when you sell, because the property tax rate is different in Penacook, as the tax section below shows.

What is the history behind Concord?

Europeans first settled the area in 1659 as Penacook, a name tied to an Abenaki word for a bend in the river. The town was incorporated as Rumford in 1734 and renamed Concord in 1765 after a boundary dispute with Bow.

Concord became the state capital in 1808, and the State House was completed in 1819. It is the oldest U.S. state capitol in which the legislature still meets in its original chambers. Concord became the Merrimack County seat in 1823.

Granite quarrying, printing and furniture-making shaped the early economy, and the Abbot-Downing company built its Concord coach from 1828. Textile mills in Penacook drew power from the Contoocook River. Many older Concord houses date from these eras, which is worth knowing if you are selling a home with original wiring, plaster walls or a stone foundation.

What are the biggest employers in Concord?

Government and healthcare dominate the Concord job market. Concord is described as a center for government, law, healthcare and insurance. The Census Bureau puts the 2025 population estimate at 44,597.

Employer (fiscal year 2020)Employees
State of New Hampshire6,069
Concord Hospital2,998
Concord School District809
City of Concord556
Lincoln Financial Group405
Market Basket405

Because so many jobs are public or hospital jobs, a Concord seller is often relocating for a new post, retiring from state service or settling the home of a parent who worked locally. Those timelines can be short, which is one reason owners look at a direct sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Concord house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How does Concord's weather affect a house?

Concord has a humid continental climate with long, cold, snowy winters. Concord Municipal Airport averages about 67.7 inches of snow and 41.95 inches of precipitation a year, and lows fall below 0 degrees Fahrenheit on about 15 nights.

The freezing period typically runs from September 27 to May 14, and about 12 days a year reach 90 degrees or higher. For a seller, that means a buyer's inspector will look hard at a few things:

  • The roof and its ability to carry a heavy snow load
  • The heating system, its age and its fuel type
  • Pipes, insulation and any sign of water intrusion
  • The foundation and drainage after spring melt

Deferred work in these areas is a common reason a financed sale stalls. A cash buyer who purchases as-is does not ask you to fix them first.

How do roads and transit shape Concord home locations?

Interstates 89 and 93 join just south of the city limits, and I-393 runs east toward the Seacoast. U.S. Route 3 serves as Main Street, and U.S. 202 and NH 9 cross the city east to west.

Concord Municipal Airport handles general aviation only. The nearest commercial airport is Manchester-Boston Regional, 23 miles south. The Concord Transportation Center at 30 Stickney Avenue, near I-93 Exit 14, serves Concord Coach Lines and Greyhound, and Concord Area Transit runs three local routes.

Passenger rail ended in 1981. Amtrak announced plans in 2021 for Boston to Concord service by 2035, which is a plan and not a service you can count on when pricing a house today.

How are Concord homes assessed and taxed?

Concord taxes homes on an April 1 to March 31 tax year, and the 2025 city rate is $29.11 per $1,000 of assessed value, or $30.74 in Penacook. The city's assessing page lists a 2025 equalization ratio of 60.4%.

ItemConcord fact
2025 tax rate, Concord$29.11 per $1,000
2025 tax rate, Penacook$30.74 per $1,000
2025 ratio60.4%
Last citywide update before 2026April 1, 2021
Late payment interest8%, prorated daily
Assessing office41 Green Street, 603-225-8550

The ratio tells you how far assessments sit from market value: total assessed value divided by the median ratio gives market value. Concord contracted with Vision Government Solutions for a full revaluation for tax year 2026, with final value notices expected the week of October 12, 2026. The city advises owners not to multiply a new assessment by the old rate, since the rate will change too.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Concord houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What does a Concord seller pay at closing?

New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax of $.75 per $100 of the price on both the buyer and the seller, under RSA 78-B. Filing and payment run through the state's Granite Tax Connect portal.

On a sale at $400,000, the arithmetic is $3,000 for each side. Your title company will show how the split is handled in your contract. Property tax is the other large line, and the city's tax year starts April 1, so ask your closing agent how the current year will be prorated.

  • Transfer tax under RSA 78-B
  • Unpaid property tax for the current tax year
  • Any mortgage or lien payoff
  • Agent commission, if you list with an agent

Deeds are recorded at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds at 163 N Main Street, Concord, phone (603) 228-0101.

What must a Concord seller disclose?

For a one to four family home, New Hampshire law requires a written seller disclosure before or during the preparation of an offer. RSA 477:4-d covers the private water supply, the private sewage system, insulation, flood hazard zone status and any underground heating oil tank.

If the seller does not know the answer on water, sewage or insulation, that has to be stated in writing. The buyer signs to acknowledge receipt. A separate rule, RSA 477:4-c, applies before any purchase contract that includes a building. It asks for details such as the system's age, its last service date and the contractor who services it. The legislature amended 477:4-d effective August 4, 2026, so use the current version of the form.

How do you contest a Concord assessment?

File an abatement application with the city by March 1 following the final tax bill. Abatements can be granted for good cause, usually an assessment error or a disproportionate assessment.

The municipality has until July 1 to grant or deny the request. If you disagree with the answer, you can appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, but not both, no later than September 1. The application does not stop collection, so pay the bill as assessed. If an abatement is granted, a refund with interest follows. The state's own guidance says statements such as "taxes too high" are not enough, so bring comparable sales or an appraisal.

During the 2026 revaluation, owners who had an informal hearing with Vision were told to expect a final-value letter in early to mid October 2026.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How does a cash sale work for a Concord house?

A cash sale replaces the lender's appraisal and underwriting with a direct purchase, so the timeline depends on title work and your own schedule. You describe the house, receive an offer, and decide whether to accept. Nothing is owed if you decline.

The state's transfer tax, the property tax proration and the disclosure form still apply to a cash deal. What changes is that you skip repairs, showings and the financing contingency. That can matter on a Concord house with an older roof, a dated heating system or an estate that has to be settled.

More questions about Concord, NH

Is Concord's property tax rate the same everywhere in the city?

No. The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000 for most of Concord and $30.74 for Penacook, which is served by the Merrimack Valley School District.

When is the deadline to appeal a Concord assessment?

The abatement application is due by March 1 following the final tax bill. The city has until July 1 to respond, and any further appeal must be filed by September 1.

Do both the buyer and the seller pay New Hampshire's transfer tax?

Yes, the statute imposes $.75 per $100 of the price on each of them. Your purchase agreement and title company set out who pays what at closing.

Does Concord have a revaluation affecting my sale?

Yes. Concord completed a full revaluation for tax year 2026, and the last citywide update before it took effect April 1, 2021. New values can change a buyer's tax estimate, so check your own notice.

Can I sell a Concord house with a private well or septic system?

Yes, but you must give the buyer the written water and sewage disclosure under RSA 477:4-d. If you do not know an answer, the law requires you to say so in writing.

Dover is the county seat of Strafford County and the most populous city in the Seacoast region. The Census Bureau estimates 34,623 residents for 2025, and Dover ranks fifth among New Hampshire cities.

The Piscataqua River forms the city's eastern boundary and the New Hampshire to Maine line. The city covers 29.04 square miles, of which 26.73 are land, and the Cochecho and Bellamy rivers drain it. Garrison Hill, about 290 feet, overlooks downtown, and Long Hill, the highest point, rises above 300 feet about three miles northwest of the center.

The neighboring municipalities matter if you are unsure which town's rules apply to a parcel near the edge of the city:

  • Newington, Durham and Madbury
  • Barrington and Rochester
  • Somersworth and Rollinsford
  • South Berwick and Eliot, Maine, across the rivers

What is Dover's history, and why does it matter for older houses?

Dover claims the oldest permanent settlement in New Hampshire, begun in 1623 when William and Edward Hilton settled at Pomeroy Cove on Dover Point. It became a city in 1855.

Cochecho Falls, with a 34-foot drop, powered sawmills and then textile mills, and the town center moved there from Dover Point. The Cocheco Manufacturing Company was founded in 1827, and in December 1828 about half of 800 women workers walked out in what is cited as the first women's strike in the United States. The railroad arrived in 1842, when the mill complex employed about 2,000 people. The millyard closed in 1937, and the city bought it at auction in 1941 for $54,000.

That industrial past left a stock of older homes close to downtown. Houses of that age often carry original wiring, old plumbing or additions built without paperwork, and those are the items a buyer's inspector tends to raise.

What does Dover's economy look like now?

The old mill complex has been reused rather than lost. Cocheco Falls Millworks now houses technology and government services companies, a restaurant, a brewery and a bar, and the Children's Museum of New Hampshire occupies a former mill.

Wentworth-Douglass Hospital is based in Dover. The city has also invested in public projects, including an $87.5 million high school and a planned $6 million waterfront development that was approved.

How do you get in and out of Dover?

Dover sits on several state routes, so commuting access is one of the first things a Dover buyer asks about. The routes are NH 4, 9, 16 (the Spaulding Turnpike), 108 and 155, plus U.S. Route 4.

Public transit is broader than in many New Hampshire cities of this size:

  • Amtrak's Downeaster stops at the Dover Transportation Center, with service to Portland, Maine, and Boston North Station
  • C&J Bus Lines runs intercity service to Boston South Station, Logan Airport and the New York Port Authority
  • COAST operates a publicly funded bus network in New Hampshire and Maine
  • Wildcat Transit serves Durham, free for UNH students and $1.50 for the public

A house within reach of the train or the Spaulding Turnpike usually has a different pool of buyers than one that is not, so mention the commute options when you describe your property.

Which school district serves Dover?

Most Dover addresses are in the Dover School District, which has about 4,000 pupils. Schools include Horne Street, Garrison and Woodman Park Elementary, Dover Middle School and Dover High School, whose teams are the Green Wave.

Private options include Saint Mary Academy, which has served the city since 1912, St. Thomas Aquinas High School at Dover Point and Portsmouth Christian Academy. Public charter schools include Cocheco Arts and Technology Academy and Seacoast Charter School. For a seller, the school assignment for your street is worth confirming with the district before you quote it to a buyer.

How is property tax set and billed in Dover?

Dover's 2025 tax rate is $19.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, certified by the New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration. The city's own rate page breaks that figure into four parts.

Component (tax year 2025)Rate per $1,000
City6.91
County1.83
State school1.16
City school9.78
Total19.68

Bills are mailed twice a year. The city's calendar sets the first half due December 1 and the second half due June 1, and says interest accrues at 12% a year after a due date. The second-half bill for 2025 was mailed May 1, 2026 and was due June 1, 2026. Exact dates can shift because the state sets the rate, so call the City Clerk and Tax Collector at 603-516-6018 before you rely on a date.

Did Dover revalue homes for 2025?

No. The assessment office did not run its annual citywide revaluation for tax year 2025, saying current values still met assessing standards and that skipping it gave a cleaner move to a new computer-assisted mass appraisal system.

The city mailed value change notices to 993 properties instead. The assessor estimated a 5% market increase for the year and said leaving values alone kept an equalization ratio of 89% to 90%. By state law, values reflect conditions on April 1, the first day of the tax year.

If you think your assessment is wrong, file an abatement application with the Tax Assessment Office by March 1 of the following year. Filing does not stop collection, so pay as billed. The assessment office is at 603-516-6014.

What happens if Dover property taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid Dover taxes can end in a lien and, eventually, a deed to the city. The city's calendar lists certified notices in July and liens recorded at the Registry of Deeds in August, with interest at 18% a year on the lien amount from the lien date.

The lien can be redeemed within two years by paying everything owed plus interest and fees. A property with an unredeemed lien can be deeded to the city at least two years and one day after the lien date. A sale is one way to clear a balance before a lien forms, and a cash buyer does not need a lender to review the arrears.

What permits and transfer costs affect a Dover sale?

Dover Inspection Services handles building permits from 269 Mast Road, next to the public works complex, and applications go through the city's online permit portal. The office can be reached at 603-516-6038.

The state codes in effect when a permit is applied for stay in force for that work, and Dover may adopt stricter building and fire codes by ordinance. If a previous owner finished a basement or added a deck, check that a permit exists before you list.

At closing, New Hampshire's transfer tax is $.75 per $100 on each of the buyer and the seller under RSA 78-B. On a $350,000 sale that is $2,625 for each. Sellers of one to four family homes must also give written disclosures on private water and sewage, insulation, flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank under RSA 477:4-d.

How does a cash sale work in Dover?

In a cash sale you describe the Dover house, receive an offer and choose whether to accept, with no obligation if you say no. There is no lender appraisal, so the repairs a financed buyer might demand do not hold up the closing.

The steps that stay the same are the title search, the tax proration and the state's transfer tax and disclosure rules.

More questions about Dover, NH

What is Dover's property tax rate?

The 2025 rate is $19.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, made up of 6.91 city, 1.83 county, 1.16 state school and 9.78 city school.

When are Dover property taxes due?

The city's calendar sets the first half due December 1 and the second half due June 1. The 2025 second-half bill was mailed May 1, 2026 and due June 1, 2026.

How do I appeal my Dover assessment?

File an abatement application with the Tax Assessment Office by March 1 following the tax bill. If the city denies it or does not act by July 1, you can appeal by September 1 to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, not both.

Is there a transfer tax when I sell a house in Dover?

Yes. New Hampshire charges $.75 per $100 of the price to each of the buyer and the seller under RSA 78-B, filed through the Granite Tax Connect portal.

Does Dover have train service for commuters?

Yes. Amtrak's Downeaster stops at the Dover Transportation Center, with service to Portland, Maine, and Boston North Station.

Where is Rochester, New Hampshire, and how is the city laid out?

Rochester is a city in Strafford County in southeastern New Hampshire. It covers 45.4 square miles, of which 45.0 is land, so a Rochester address can mean anything from a downtown lot to a rural road with acreage.

The city is drained by the Salmon Falls, Isinglass and Cochecho rivers. The high point is Chestnut Hill at 581 feet in the northern corner. The Census Bureau counted 32,492 residents in 2020, which made Rochester the sixth largest city in the state, and the estimate for July 1, 2025 is 33,716.

Three villages sit inside the city limits, and each has its own feel when a buyer or an appraiser looks at a house:

  • East Rochester
  • Gonic
  • North Rochester

Because the villages are part of the City of Rochester, they share one assessing department and one tax collector.

How did Rochester start, and why does that matter for old houses?

Rochester was chartered as a town on May 10, 1722, by Governor Samuel Shute, and it became a city in 1891. The original grant was a ten-mile square of about 64,000 acres that helped screen the older coastal settlements from the north.

Lumbering came first. The Cochecho River then powered mills, and six tanneries were running by 1806. Shoe making passed textiles as the leading industry by 1880. The E.G. and E. Wallace Shoe Company, founded in 1854, had more than 700 workers by 1901, and Kessel Fire Brick opened in 1889. Four railroads once met here on the line between Haverhill, Massachusetts, and Portland, Maine.

Hubbard Shoe closed in 1973 and Maybury Shoe in the mid-1970s. A fire in October 1947 destroyed more than 30 homes, so some blocks were rebuilt at the same time.

What are the main roads, transit and employers around Rochester?

The Spaulding Turnpike, NH Route 16, is the main artery. It is a six-lane, controlled-access highway through Rochester that runs south toward Dover and Portsmouth and north toward Conway. NH Route 125 crosses the center of town north to south, NH Route 11 runs west to Alton and Laconia, NH Route 108 heads southeast to Dover, and NH Route 202A runs southwest toward Strafford and Northwood. US 202 bypasses the city center.

Rochester Skyhaven Airport is inside the city, and the Cooperative Alliance for Seacoast Transportation (COAST) runs local buses.

Employers named in public sources include Frisbie Memorial Hospital, Albany International, Market Basket, Walmart, Lowe's, Kohl's, The Home Depot, Hannaford, Laars Heating Systems, Lydall Performance Materials, the City of Rochester and the Rochester School District. A New Hampshire Employment Security profile, which uses 2013 figures and is dated, found that 33.3 percent of working residents had jobs in Rochester, 59.7 percent worked in another New Hampshire town and 7 percent worked out of state, with a mean commute of 25 minutes.

What kinds of homes do Rochester sellers usually have?

Rochester has a wide mix of housing types, and the mix affects how a sale works. The 2008-2012 American Community Survey, as reported by the state, counted 14,003 housing units in the city. These are the largest groups:

  • 7,392 single-family homes, attached or detached
  • 2,061 units in buildings of two to four units
  • 2,035 units in buildings of five or more
  • 2,515 mobile homes and other units

That is an older count, but it shows that manufactured housing is a meaningful share of the city. It also explains why the 2024 revaluation drew attention: the mayor said some mobile home values had doubled and sometimes almost tripled.

Owners of two- to four-unit buildings often sell with tenants in place. If you are in that position, tell any buyer early what leases exist and when the rent is paid. A cash buyer can take occupied property, but the lease terms and notice rules under New Hampshire law still apply.

What are Rochester's property tax rate and bill dates?

The 2025 Rochester tax rate is $15.30 per $1,000 of assessed value, set by the New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration. It was $14.85 in 2024 and $25.74 in 2023. The 2025 rate breaks down as follows, with net assessed valuation of $5.185 billion:

Component2025 rate per $1,000
City$4.45
County$1.77
Local school$7.98
State school$1.10
Total$15.30

Rochester bills twice a year. The June 2026 bills were mailed June 10 and were due July 10, 2026. The December 2025 bills were mailed December 18, and the last day to pay before interest started was January 20, 2026. The city's tax collector is at 150 Wakefield Street, Suite 271, and takes payment in person, by mail, online (for an added fee), through bank bill pay and in a night drop box. A returned payment, including a returned eCheck, costs $25.

The 2025 increase of $0.45 meant about $169.65 more on a median single-family value of $377,000, according to the city.

What did the 2024 revaluation change for Rochester owners?

Rochester completed a citywide revaluation effective April 1, 2024, and the tax rate fell 42.3 percent because values rose sharply. The prior full revaluation was in 2019, and the state requires one at least every five years.

The revaluation added $2.3 billion to the city's net assessed valuation. The city said a higher value does not automatically produce a higher bill: homes that had been assessed well below market moved up the most, while homes already near market value changed little and some owners paid less. The 2024 rate of $14.85 was the lowest among nearby communities the city compared, with Somersworth at $18.70, Dover at $18.17 and Newmarket at $17.20.

The city's median sales ratio, which compares assessments to actual sale prices, was 97.4 percent for 2024 and 93.2 percent for 2025. For a seller, a ratio below 100 percent means sale prices are running somewhat above assessed values. Before the revaluation the ratio had been 64.3 percent for 2022, so older assessed values said very little about what a house would fetch.

How do you contest a Rochester assessment?

You apply for an abatement with the city, and under RSA 76:16 the application is due by March 1 following the date of the tax notice. Only a person aggrieved by the assessment can apply, and the owner must have complied with RSA 74.

The assessors must grant or deny the application in writing by July 1 after the notice date. If they do not respond, the law treats that as a denial. A written decision has to explain the appeal route.

If you disagree with the result, RSA 76:16-a lets you appeal on or before September 1 to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals. The filing fee is $65, and you may choose a small claims procedure unless the city asks for a full hearing. Rochester's Assessing Department answers questions at (603) 332-5109 and offers appointments online.

The steps in order:

  1. Read the assessment notice and compare it with recent sales of similar homes.
  2. Ask the Assessing Department to review your record.
  3. File the abatement application by March 1.
  4. Wait for the written decision, due by July 1.
  5. If needed, appeal by September 1.

What local rules and costs apply when a Rochester house sells?

New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax of $0.75 per $100 of the price, and both the buyer and the seller pay it. The state collects it through the Granite Tax Connect portal, and the Department of Revenue Administration call center is at (603) 230-5920.

The city's Building and Licensing Services office, at the City Hall Annex, 33 Wakefield Street, enforces these codes. Call (603) 332-3508 with questions about open permits or unfinished work:

  • International Building Code, 2021 edition
  • International Residential Code, 2021 edition
  • International Energy Conservation Code, 2018 edition
  • National Electrical Code, 2023 edition, effective July 1, 2025
  • International Property Maintenance Code, 2015 edition
  • Life Safety Code and State Fire Code, enforced by the Fire Department

Open permits and unfinished work are worth checking before any sale, whether conventional or cash.

Which schools serve Rochester?

The Rochester School District, SAU 54, runs the city's public schools from its office at 150 Wakefield Street, Suite 200. Its listed schools are Spaulding High School, Rochester Middle School, McClelland Elementary, Bud Carlson Academy, Chamberlain Street School, East Rochester School, Gonic School and Salmon Falls School.

How does a cash sale of a Rochester house work?

In a cash sale, a buyer purchases the house without a mortgage, so the timeline depends on title work and your schedule instead of a lender's appraisal. You tell us about the property, we review it, and we send a written offer. You may decline it and owe nothing.

Cash buyers purchase houses as-is, so repairs, old furnishings and deferred maintenance stay with the buyer. At closing, a New Hampshire title or closing attorney pays off any mortgage and any property tax owed from the proceeds, and records the deed with the registry of deeds for Strafford County.

A cash sale does not suit every owner. If your house is in good shape and you have time, a listing may bring a higher price. If you inherited it, are behind on payments, have tenants or face costly repairs, speed and certainty may matter more.

More questions about Rochester, NH

What is the property tax rate in Rochester, NH?

The 2025 rate is $15.30 per $1,000 of assessed value: $4.45 city, $1.77 county, $7.98 local school and $1.10 state school. The state sets the 2026 rate in late fall.

When are Rochester property taxes due?

Rochester bills twice a year. The June 2026 bills were due July 10, 2026, and the December 2025 bills could be paid without interest through January 20, 2026. Check your bill for the exact date.

Can I sell my Rochester house if I owe property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the closing attorney handles it. Call the Tax Collector at 150 Wakefield Street for a payoff figure.

What is the New Hampshire transfer tax on a house sale?

The state charges $0.75 per $100 of the price, and both the buyer and the seller pay it.

How do I appeal my Rochester assessment?

File an abatement application with the city by March 1 after the tax notice. If the city denies it, appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals by September 1.
